cd /Users/ccheever/bench-matrix-20260823-r2/cells/opus-clique-explicit && cat > diary.md <<'EOF'
# diary.md — lane opus-clique-explicit (Clique on Snapback 0.1.25, explicit profile)

## M1 — accounts and profiles

### What I built

- A Snapback backend in the **default explicit profile**: `snapback/schema.mjs`
  with a `defineAuth` program (password credentials on the built-in provider,
  `minimumLength: 8`, no guest arm, no email-code arm) and eleven tables;
  `snapback/functions.mjs` with `defineJsLiveQuery` / `defineJsMutation` /
  `defineAssetUpload` declarations and generated exact function references
  under `snapback/generated/`.
- An Expo Router web client on top of the frozen UI kit (vendored verbatim into
  `src/social-ui/`), with a persistent nav rail (feed tabs + chats list) and a
  routed main column, so the contract's `sm-feed-tab-*` and `sm-chats-item`
  IDs stay reachable from every route the choreography visits.
- A **fixture replay adapter** (`tools/replay.mjs`) that installs
  `starter-m1.log` through the app's real signup and mutation paths — ~1,000
  password hashes is the M6 shape; here it is 8 — plus a `seedRefs` ledger
  table so a second run of the same segment is a no-op.
- A one-command acceptance suite (`npm run acceptance -- --milestone m1`)
  that seeds, runs the milestone's suite-required assertions against the real
  web client, validates a coverage manifest against the instrument's
  `assertions.json`, and writes the suite receipt, the choreography
  suite-status linkage, and the typed D0.6 observation sidecar.

### What felt easy

- **Codegen diagnostics are unusually good.** Every refusal named its rule, a
  source span, an admitted alternative, and a build-bound guide anchor. When
  the inline handler profile rejected `obj[key]`, the message told me the exact
  rule (`inline.syntax.forbidden`), the exact line, and the page to read. I
  never had to guess.
- **The served Guide is a real product.** `snapback guide <query>` plus
  `GET /_snapback/guide/<page>.md` off the running binary meant documentation
  was build-bound to the binary I was actually running, and section flats let
  me pull "backend" and "clients" once instead of grepping a wiki.
- **Password auth is genuinely built in.** `defineAuth` + `signUpWithPassword`
  / `signInWithPassword` / `signOut` gave me M1's whole auth surface — server
  hashing, one-time recovery codes, server-side logout revocation — without me
  writing a KDF or a session table. That is the single biggest hour saved.
- **Live queries are the default shape.** `profileByHandle` is thirty lines of
  declaration and the other client saw a profile edit in ~300 ms with no
  subscription plumbing on my side.

### What fought me

- **Random ports in the paved dev loop.** `snapback dev --expo` picks free
  loopback ports for Metro's front proxy and the supervisor bootstrap origin,
  which collides with this lane's fixed 42160–42179 constraint. I ended up
  running the backend with `--external-client-origin` and hand-building the
  `supervised-dev` AppBindingV1 in `src/backend.tsx`. That took reading
  `app-client.mjs` to learn that the binding's `capabilities.offered` must
  include `auth.passwords`, which no page states.
- **`custody: 'volatile-explicit'`.** The expo-chat template ships it, AGENTS.md
  tells you not to move off it, and it silently selects *memory* auth custody —
  so the session does not survive a reload, which is M1 acceptance item 3. The
  guide text says Expo web "has the same durable reload restoration as React
  web", which is true only under `durable-required`. I had to read
  `app-client.mjs` to find the selector.
- **Inline handler admission.** Computed member access and top-level `const`
  capture are both refused. My first `functions.mjs` used plain objects as maps
  everywhere; converting to `Map`/`Set` was mechanical but unexpected, and the
  rule is a page I had not been routed to by the start packet.
- **A two-step signup.** Snapback owns the principal; my app owns the profile
  row with the unique handle. That makes "duplicate handle is rejected with a
  visible error" a two-server-step story: a public pre-check query, then the
  unique index as the real authority. It works and it is honest, but it is more
  ceremony than a single `createUser({handle})`.

### What the explicit profile saved or cost

- **Saved:** every function is a value I can read. `results.records(v.object({…}))`
  made the wire contract of each screen explicit, and the generated
  `api.d.ts` typed the client without me writing a single interface twice. The
  `refusals: [...]` + `ctx.refuse(code)` channel is the thing I miss most in
  other backends: `HANDLE_TAKEN` arrives at the browser as a stable code, not a
  message I have to regex.
- **Cost:** the declaration is verbose and the handler dialect is a subset of
  JavaScript. `Object.keys(map).map(k => map[k])` is not admissible; neither is
  a shared `const MAX_ROWS`. I paid maybe 25 minutes to that dialect. The
  `authScopeField` declaration also refused my computed-record field name
  (`FUNCTION_UNKNOWN_FIELD` — it must name a *table* field), so principal-scoped
  handler queries currently carry no scope declaration at all.

### What documentation or diagnostic was missing

1. **No page tells you which capabilities a hand-built AppBinding must offer.**
   `auth.passwords` is only discoverable by reading
   `@expo/snapback-client/app-client.mjs`. A "run Expo against a fixed-port
   backend" recipe would have saved the whole detour.
2. **`custody` is documented as a posture, not as a mechanism.** Nothing says
   "volatile-explicit means memory custody, so reload loses the session."
3. **`authScopeField` on handler-backed live queries.** The guide describes it
   as declaring "which result field represents the principal", but codegen
   validates it against the primary table's fields. Either the prose or the
   validator is wrong; with a computed record contract there is no way to
   declare it at all.
4. **The instrument's choreography cannot install its own dependencies** when
   the instrument tree is read-only; a lane-side resolver shim was needed. That
   is an instrument-packaging gap, not a Snapback one.

### M1 result

Suite 7/7 suite-required assertions, coverage 7/7. Choreography segment `m1`
3/3 required assertions passed, `green: true`, `nonGreenCause: null`.
EOF

content.content:
## What arrives: replace and delta

Two vocabularies meet here, and they are not the same list. **Wire frames**
on the durable lane carry one of five kinds: `live_replace` (a full snapshot
of the result), `live_delta` (incremental add/remove — the analyzable
unordered/filtered subset gets deltas; ordered queries fall back to
replace; LLP 0008 §DK-3), `resync_required` (the client must re-snapshot),
`authorization_invalidation` (the auth barrier —
[protecting data](../auth/protecting-data.md)), and `current_as_of` (the
answer to a resume-token subscribe: version advances, rows untouched).
Two of those never reach your callback as-is: the client consumes
`resync_required` by re-snapshotting, and it consumes
`authorization_invalidation` internally, resurfacing the boundary as the
`authorization_*` events below.

**What your `onUpdate(rows, meta)` receives** is different. A plain
(non-auth-scoped) subscription sees `meta.kind: 'live_replace'` or
`'live_delta'` (plus `'current_as_of'` when it resumed from a token). An
auth-scoped subscription — anything gated by a membership predicate or
another protected-query input — delivers through the witnessed lane instead
and never sees a bare `live_replace`. Its `meta.kind` values are this closed
set; handle all five:

- `authorization_snapshot` — an auth-verified result snapshot;
- `authorization_quarantine` — the result blanked at a governed boundary
  (e.g. the caller leaves the membership), awaiting a fresh satisfying
  snapshot or a trusted denial;
- `authorization_delete` — the terminal denial: rows deleted, fresh reads
  stay denied ([protecting data](../auth/protecting-data.md) describes the
  quarantine→delete ladder);
- `authorization_error` — the boundary machinery itself faulted; the handle
  blanks and the connection reports stale;
- `authorization_denied` — a server-answered denial on a fresh subscribe or
  authority transition; the same fact freezes on
  `handle.authorizationDenial` for rendering.

Incremental publication also requires the query's exact, schema-derived
`Documents` result contract. A `live_delta` publishes committed storage rows
without rerunning the complete query, so a `Documents` tag, table name, or
hand-written narrower descriptor is not enough to prove that those rows match
the operation's egress contract. Codegen supplies the exact contract and hash
for an ordinary authored declarative query. Internal fixtures that construct a
function manifest directly must derive the contract through the same codegen
path, as the linked executable fixture does; do not invent a descriptor by
hand. A missing or non-exact contract does not make the live query unloadable:
the server honestly takes the full re-query plus `live_replace` path instead.

When an apparently analyzable query receives replacements, check all of the
conservative boundaries together: ordered or limited queries, membership-gated
queries, generated standard patterns, opaque handlers, and manifests without
the exact schema-derived document contract are replace-only. This fallback is
intentional and correctness-preserving, not evidence that durable push failed.

The kit's end-to-end delta witness
(`demos/_kit/tests/live-delta-e2e.mjs`) drives all of this over a real
socket. Its subscription records every delivered `meta.kind`:

```js source=demos/_kit/tests/live-delta-e2e.mjs
  const handle = await db.liveQuery('listMine', {
    connectionId: 'delta_conn',
    userId: ADA,
    transport: 'stream',
    stream: { heartbeatIntervalMs: 200, freshnessBudgetMs: 800, reconnectBaseDelayMs: 100, reconnectMaxDelayMs: 400 },
    onUpdate: rec.onUpdate,
  });
```

and it asserts a matching insert arrived as a delta, not a replace:

```js source=demos/_kit/tests/live-delta-e2e.mjs
      const delta = rec.updates.find((u) => u.kind === 'live_delta');
      assert(delta, `expected a live_delta update; saw kinds ${rec.updates.map((u) => u.kind)}`);
```

Membership-gated live replacement does not make a query safe for offline
retention. V1 refuses retained role-gated queries until an authorized lease can
bind the exact membership declaration/resource dependency and expiry floor.
For online live state, declaration-bound `requireRole` dependencies are
revocation-active: resource- or app-scoped membership deletion/downgrade first
blanks the established result, then a trusted denial terminally deletes it and
ACKs the exact obligation. Fresh reads remain denied and later writes cannot
repopulate that handle.

## Connection state an author can observe

The stream manager emits `'connecting'`, `'open'`, `'lost'`
(`{ wasOpen }`), `'budget-missed'` (socket claims open but the freshness
budget lapsed), and `'closed'`. The kit derives a per-query `connection`
axis from these and pushes it through `onConnectionChange`; the conventional
author-facing mapping (from the cursors-web hook) is:

```ts source=demos/cursors-web/surfaces/react/src/useCursorRoom.ts
export type ConnectionAxis = 'connecting' | 'live' | 'stale' | 'disconnected';
```

`open → live`; `budget-missed`/`lost → stale` (degraded — render retained
data, marked); `closed → disconnected`. Defaults:
`LIVE_HEARTBEAT_INTERVAL_MS = 5_000`, `LIVE_FRESHNESS_BUDGET_MS = 15_000`,
reconnect backoff 250ms → 10s. The
[headless client](../clients/headless.md) owns this state machine; the
[Contract adapter](../clients/contract-adapter.md) and React arm consume it.

## Ask whether a principal has a fresh client

# Clique

A group messaging and social app (accounts, profiles, a follow graph, post
feeds, and WhatsApp-shaped messaging) built as an **Expo Router** client on a
**Snapback 0.1.25** backend authored in the **default explicit profile**
(`snapback/schema.mjs` + `snapback/functions.mjs` with generated exact function
references under `snapback/generated/`).

Scope built here: **M1 (accounts and profiles), M2 (posts and the follow
graph), M3 (messaging core)** of the `social-messenger` brief.

## Layout

| Path | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| `snapback/schema.mjs` | Auth program (email + password, built-in provider) and every table |
| `snapback/functions.mjs` | Live queries, mutations, and asset upload intents |
| `snapback/surface-model.mjs` | The ephemeral `typing` presence collection |
| `app/` | Expo Router routes (feed, thread, profile, settings, chats, search) |
| `src/social-ui/` | The frozen social-messenger UI kit, vendored verbatim (`src/social-ui/UI-KIT-VERSION`) |
| `src/` | App shell, data hooks, asset/media helpers |
| `tools/replay.mjs` | Fixture action-log replay adapter (the app's own write path) |
| `tools/acceptance.mjs` | The acceptance suite entrypoint |

## Running it

Two servers, both inside this lane's pinned port range:

```sh
# 1. backend (port 42160)
npm run dev

# 2. Expo web client (port 42161)
npm run web
```

`npm run dev` is `snapback dev snapback --port 42160 --external-client-origin
http://127.0.0.1:42161`. The client builds its deployment binding from the
generated descriptor plus `EXPO_PUBLIC_CLIQUE_BACKEND` (default
`http://127.0.0.1:42160`) — see `src/backend.tsx`.

## Acceptance

One documented command per milestone, from a clean checkout against the running
backend and web client:

```sh
npm run acceptance -- --milestone m1
npm run acceptance -- --milestone m2
npm run acceptance -- --milestone m3
```

Each run:

1. installs that milestone's fixture action-log segments through the app's own
   signup and mutation paths, twice, so seed idempotency is measured rather
   than asserted;
2. executes every **suite-required** assertion for that milestone from the
   instrument's `schema/social-messenger/assertions.json`, against the real web
   client and the real backend;
3. validates a coverage manifest — every suite-required assertion must map to a
   test, and the run fails if any is unmapped;
4. writes `../receipts/<mN>-suite.json` (results plus the coverage map),
   `../receipts/<mN>-suite.observations.jsonl` (typed D0.6 observations), and
   the `../suite-status.json` linkage the choreography harness reads before it
   starts a browser.

Exit code `0` means every suite-required assertion passed and coverage is
complete.

`CLIQUE_REGRESSION=1 npm run acceptance -- --milestone mN` runs the same suite
into `regression-*` receipts without disturbing an already-signalled milestone.

## Two-client choreography

The frozen instrument harness runs unmodified from the read-only instrument
tree; `tools/choreo-register.mjs` is a resolve hook that satisfies its single
bare specifier (`playwright`) from this lane's pinned install.

```sh
CHOREO_BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:42161 \
CHOREO_ALICE_PASSWORD='...' CHOREO_BOB_PASSWORD='...' \
node --import ./tools/choreo-register.mjs \
  <instrument>/tools/social-messenger/choreography/choreography.mjs m3 \
  --lane-run-id opus-clique-explicit \
  --suite-status ../suite-status.json \
  --receipts ../receipts/m3-choreography.jsonl
```

## Seeding

```sh
npm run seed -- starter-m1.log starter-m2.log starter-m3.log
```

Replay is idempotent per installed segment: `snapback/functions.mjs` keeps a
`seedRefs` ledger mapping each action-log id to the server-owned entity it
created, so a second run of the same segment creates nothing.

## Other scripts

- `npm run generate` — regenerate `snapback/generated/` after editing the
  backend declarations.
- `npm run typecheck` — TypeScript over the app and the vendored kit.
- `npx expo export --platform ios` — the per-milestone iOS Hermes bundle
  artifact (`../artifacts/ios-export-mN`).
EOF

input.command:
cat >> diary.md <<'EOF'

## M3 — messaging core

### What I built

- DMs deduplicated by a `pairKey` on a **unique index over an optional field** —
  present only for DMs, so the constraint applies to pairs and never to groups,
  and "starting the same DM again" resolves to the existing channel inside the
  mutation instead of racing at the client.
- Groups as first-class entities (name, description, admin/member roles,
  add/remove/promote), with two identical-membership groups deliberately
  coexisting because nothing dedupes them.
- Quoted replies as a pointer (`messages.quoteId`), rendered through the kit's
  `QuotedReply`, with a lane-owned `sm-convo-bubble` wrapper so the contract's
  per-message actions resolve *inside* the bubble the harness selected.
- Receipts as **per-membership watermarks** (`deliveredSeq` / `readSeq`) rather
  than per-message rows: the aggregate is `min` over the recipient set at send
  time, and a member who leaves has no row and so drops out of the requirement.
  That is one row per member per chat instead of one per message per member.
- Typing as the template's ephemeral collection, retuned to a 3 s lease so the
  brief's "expires within 5 s of the last keystroke" holds even if a publisher
  stalls.

### What felt easy

- **Ephemeral presence is a genuinely small surface.** `ephemeral.collection`
  plus `useSnapbackPresence` with a `skip` sentinel for observers was maybe
  twenty lines for a correct typing indicator with server-owned expiry. I have
  hand-rolled this three times in other stacks and it was never twenty lines.
- **Unique indexes over optional fields.** `pairKey` optional + `{unique:true}`
  expresses "at most one DM per pair, unlimited groups" as one declaration.
  Codegen derived `whereApplicable` and I did not have to think about it again.
- **Declared refusals paid off again.** `m3-a14` ("a non-admin cannot remove
  members") asserts the exact `NOT_ADMIN` app code at the API *and* the visible
  error in the UI, and both come from one `ctx.refuse('NOT_ADMIN')`.

### What fought me

- **`useSnapbackMutation` returns a union.** `String(await createGroup(...))`
  produced `"[object Object]"` and the new group's route was unreachable. My
  mistake, but the failure mode is silent: navigation to a nonsense id renders
  "this conversation is unavailable" rather than anything that points at the
  dispatch shape.
- **`SNAPBACK_OUTBOX_AUTHORIZATION_SUSPENDED`.** Both non-queued dispatch forms
  refuse with "foreground mutation waits for authorization proof" while the
  client is re-establishing authority after a route change. It says *waits*; it
  *refuses*, and the caller has to wait. It is effect-free (raised before
  transport dispatch), so a bounded retry over the closed authority-fence code
  set is safe — but I only convinced myself of that by reading the published
  client source.
- **The 2 s typing ceiling caught a rendering bug, not a backend one.** Every
  keystroke re-rendered the whole message list, so typing a 45-character string
  cost ~60 ms per character and the indicator appeared 2.77 s after the first
  keystroke. Isolating the draft into a memoized composer took it to ~1.4 s
  (single-keystroke latency ~72 ms). The backend was never the problem — but
  the instrument's ceiling is what exposed it.

### What the explicit profile saved or cost

- **Saved:** the receipt model. Because `chatMessages` is one declared handler
  with a declared read set, "when does a receipt tick change?" is a function of
  `memberships` — one line in `reads`, and the aggregate is computed in the same
  place it is defined. In a fetch-shaped backend this is where I would have
  started inventing cache invalidation.
- **Cost:** the same handler dialect tax, plus one structural cost I did not
  expect: `authScopeField` cannot name a computed record field, so none of my
  principal-dependent live queries carry a scope declaration. The gate is real
  (`ctx.auth` inside the handler), but the platform's own invalidation and
  retention bookkeeping does not know these queries are per-principal.

### What documentation or diagnostic was missing

1. **The dispatch-shape choice is not presented as a decision.** `useSnapbackMutation`
   (union), `{queue:false}` (strict, refuses on unsettled authority),
   `useSnapbackSettledMutation` (settled convenience, same refusal) — there is
   no table saying which one an ordinary online screen should use, and the two
   that "resolve the result" both have the same sharp edge.
2. **`SNAPBACK_OUTBOX_AUTHORIZATION_SUSPENDED` has no guide entry** describing
   caller obligation. `snapback guide <CODE>` returned the registry stub
   (subsystem + HTTP status) and nothing about what to do.
3. **`authScopeField` and handler-backed live queries** (repeated from M1): the
   documented meaning ("which *result* field represents the principal") and the
   validator (a *table* field) disagree.

### M3 result

Suite 7/7 suite-required assertions, coverage 7/7. Choreography segment `m3`:
both required checks passed plus the optional quoted-reply excerpt-and-jump
check, four assertions skipped by the frozen contract (no sender-avatar ID, no
semantic receipt token, no group-member lifecycle controls), `green: true`,
`nonGreenCause: null`.

### Cross-milestone regression

After M3 I re-ran all three suites and all three choreography segments on the
final build: M1 7/7, M2 22/22, M3 7/7, and `m1`/`m2`/`m3` choreography all
`green: true` (`receipts/regression-*`). `tsc --noEmit` is clean.
EOF
echo ok; wc -l diary.md

input.command: cat > essay.md <<'EOF' # Building Clique on Snapback — a comparison with backends I know *Written after M1–M3 of the `social-messenger` brief, before any numbers were tallied. Lane `opus-clique-explicit`; Snapback 0.1.25, default explicit authoring profile; Expo Router web client on the frozen UI kit.* --- ## The shape of the thing Snapback is not a database with an API bolted on, and it is not a function-as-a-service with a database attached. It is a **declared application**: a schema module and a functions module that together compile to an artifact with a hash, and a running binary that will only serve the artifact you declared. The first consequence is that there is no "the backend" separate from "my code" — the generated `api.mjs` I import in React is the same identity the server loaded, and the client refuses to attach if they disagree. I have never had a stack tell me "your bundle is one generation ahead of the backend" as a first-class, recoverable state. Metro handed me exactly that twice and it retried itself. The second consequence is that everything interesting is a *value in a file*. A live query is `defineJsLiveQuery({ args, auth, reads, result, handler })`. Its result contract is `results.records(v.object({...}))`. Its invalidation surface is the `reads` array. When I wanted to know why my feed was not updating, the question "what does this query depend on?" had an answer I could read, not a cache-key convention I had to reconstruct. ## Against Convex Convex is the closest relative and the comparison is the most interesting. Convex's `useQuery` is *automatically* reactive: you write a query function, you call `useQuery`, and reactivity is a property of the whole system. Snapback splits it — `defineQuery` is callable, `defineLiveQuery` is subscribable, and a client that subscribes to the wrong one gets `SNAPBACK_FUNCTION_NOT_LIVE` rather than a silent poll. I liked this more than I expected to. Marking a query live is a cost decision (a subscription, an invalidation dependency), and Snapback makes you spend it deliberately. On this app, `feedPage`, `chatMessages`, `myChats`, and `profileByHandle` are live; nothing else is, and I can see that at a glance. Where Convex is clearly ahead is the authoring dialect. Convex handlers are ordinary TypeScript. Snapback's inline handler profile is a **subset**: no computed member access (`obj[key]`), no captured top-level `const`, no classes, no imports; same-file `function` declarations are spliced in and everything else is refused at generation. I rewrote every map in `functions.mjs` as a `Map` and every membership test as a `Set`. That is maybe half an hour across the whole build, and the diagnostics are excellent (`SNAPBACK_INLINE_HANDLER_SYNTAX_FORBIDDEN` with a source span, the admitted alternative, and a guide anchor), but it is a real tax and it will surprise anyone arriving from Convex. Where Snapback is clearly ahead of Convex is **auth as a declared program**. Convex gives you an auth *integration* — you bring Clerk or Auth0 or WorkOS. Snapback's `defineAuth` gave me email + password with server-side hashing, one-time recovery codes, server-side logout revocation, and a durable browser custody carrier, in about forty lines of declaration and no third party. For a brief that puts OAuth and email delivery explicitly out of scope, that is the single biggest hour saved in this build. Convex would have had me shipping a provider integration or hand-rolling argon2id. The other Snapback advantage over Convex is **declared refusals**. `refusals: ['NOT_ADMIN', 'HANDLE_TAKEN', …]` + `ctx.refuse(code, details)` gives the client a stable application code that the host will only admit if the function declared it. My acceptance suite asserts `appCode === 'NOT_ADMIN'` rather than matching a message. In Convex I would be throwing `ConvexError` with a payload I invented, which works but is a convention rather than a contract. ## Against Supabase Supabase's model is Postgres plus RLS plus PostgREST, and the comparison is mostly about *where the boundary lives*. In Supabase the boundary is the row policy: the client talks to the table, and the policy decides. Snapback has table `visibility` too, but the reachable surface is *only the functions you declared* — there is no generic table endpoint at all. That changes the shape of a security review. In Supabase I audit policies and then worry about which columns leak through a `select *`. Here I audit function declarations, and a table nobody declared a function over is simply unreachable. I used `public-read` visibility on Clique's tables and put membership scoping in the query handlers (`chatMessages` returns nothing to a non-member). In Supabase I would have written that as an RLS policy and gotten defence in depth. That is a genuine Supabase advantage and I want to be honest that my posture here is weaker than a policy-backed one would be: Snapback ships a `membership` visibility kind and I did not use it, because wiring the membership declaration was more risk than the M1–M3 assertions required. If I were shipping this, that is the first thing I would go back and do. Supabase's realtime is also a fair fight and Snapback wins it. Supabase Realtime gives you row-level change feeds; you still assemble the *view*. Snapback delivers the query's result — my feed row is a joined, viewer-scoped record with like counts, repost attribution, and the viewer's own like state, and the client receives that shape, not four table streams to reduce. Measured on this app, a new post reached the other browser in ~270 ms end to end with no code of mine in the path. Where Supabase is far ahead: **operations and escape hatches**. It is Postgres. I can open psql. I can write a recursive CTE, a materialized view, a partial index, a trigger. Snapback's bounded query builder (`.eq/.in/.lt/.gt/.order/.take`) is deliberately small; `take()` caps at 1,024 rows and refuses an unbounded `collect()` outright, which is *right* for correctness-at-scale and occasionally maddening when you know exactly what you want. My "viewer's own likes" projection is two bounded set reads with an honest 1,024-row ceiling; in Postgres it is a semi-join and I would not have thought about it. ## Against Firebase Firebase is the one Clique most resembles in product shape, and the comparison is lopsided. Firestore's security rules are a separate language with a separate mental model and a famously bad debugging story; Snapback's authorization is `auth: 'authenticated'` on the function plus `ctx.auth.userId` in the handler, and when I got it wrong the failure was a typed refusal, not an empty result set. Firestore also pushes you toward denormalization because queries cannot join — which is exactly the trap I fell into anyway when I denormalized follower counts, and then had to take back. Snapback let me derive those counts at read time inside the query, and the live invalidation followed the derivation for free. What Firebase still has that Snapback does not: a hosted production story I can point a real user at today. Snapback's own guide is scrupulous about this — every page I read carried a "Local target only" banner and the auth pages say plainly that there is no production email delivery and no self-serve hosted identity. That honesty is admirable and it is also a hard limit. Clique runs on my machine. ## Against hand-rolled Postgres + Express This is the baseline I know best, and it is the comparison where Snapback's value is easiest to quantify. To reach M1–M3 by hand I would have written: a migration system, a users/sessions schema, argon2id wiring, a session middleware, a refresh/rotation story, a logout revocation path, ~25 REST endpoints with validation, a WebSocket layer, a subscription registry, an invalidation strategy, an asset upload pipeline with content-type sniffing and EXIF stripping, a delivery route with caching, and a client cache. Optimistically two weeks. Here the equivalent is roughly 1,300 lines of `functions.mjs` and 220 lines of `schema.mjs`, and I spent my actual debugging time on *my own React memoization bug*, not on any of that infrastructure. The specific thing I would not get back by hand is the **asset pipeline**. One `defineAssetUpload` with `delivery: 'public-immutable'` and an image variant, one `v.assetRef` field, one `ctx.assets.attach` line, and `useSnapbackAssetImage` rendering the delivery ladder — including holding the placeholder until the rendition publishes so a plain `` never flashes a 404. Two fixture images and a playing MP4 with zero URL construction on my side. I have written that pipeline badly at least twice. ## What actually cost me time Three things, and none of them were the backend's data model. 1. **A memoization mistake in my own React code** that hid field-only live updates while insert/delete updates worked. What made it tractable was that Snapback has two client arms: I ran the same live query headlessly, proved the server delivered the change in under a second, and knew immediately the bug was mine. That two-arm property is underrated as a debugging tool. 2. **Composition at the edges of the paved path.** `snapback dev --expo` picks random loopback ports; my lane pins a port range; so I hand-built the deployment binding and discovered by reading the published client source that it must offer `auth.passwords`. Everything about the binding is validated and the diagnostics are precise — but there is no recipe for "Expo against a fixed-port backend", and that composition took longer than any schema work. 3. **Dispatch shape and authority fences.** `useSnapbackMutation` returns a union; the two variants that resolve a plain result both refuse with `SNAPBACK_OUTBOX_AUTHORIZATION_SUSPENDED` while authority is settling. That refusal is effect-free and a bounded retry is correct, but I established that by reading `@expo/snapback-client`'s source rather than a page. ## The overall impression Snapback feels like a backend designed by people who have been burned by silent failure. Almost everything refuses rather than degrades: an unbounded collect refuses, an undeclared refusal code folds to generic, a mismatched artifact refuses to attach, a required field cannot be dropped without a migration, a supervised binding expires. Working inside that is occasionally slow and never mysterious. The counterweight is that when something *is* mysterious — my stale rows, the authority-suspended refusal — the observability to diagnose it is not there yet: `status: ready, freshness: current, connection: live` while serving a stale row is the one moment in three milestones where the platform told me nothing useful and I had to build my own instrument. If I were choosing for a real product with this shape today, I would pick Convex for the authoring ergonomics if I already had an identity provider, Supabase if I needed SQL escape hatches or a hosted deployment tomorrow, and Snapback if I wanted the *whole* app — auth, live queries, presence, assets, offline retention — to be one declared artifact with one identity and no third parties. On the strength of M1–M3, the third option is a real option, which is not something I would have said about a 0.1.x backend going in. EOF wc -w essay.md

## 6. What is built, and what is not

**Built and green (M1–M3).** Email + password accounts on Snapback's built-in
provider with server-side hashing, one-time recovery codes, durable browser
session custody and server-side logout revocation; the brief's exact profile
field set with a server-enforced unique handle and fixture avatar upload;
text/image/video posts with a bounded ordered media child table; follow graph
with derived counts; likes, reposts and replies as idempotent set-state intents;
Following and Global feeds with keyset paging and implicit self-follow; post
threads; DMs deduplicated per pair; groups with roles and membership
administration; text messages with quoted replies; typing presence inside the
brief's 2 s/5 s ceilings; monotonic per-member receipt watermarks with
recipient-set-at-send-time aggregation; people search with the brief's
case-insensitive word-prefix semantics; and a versioned, idempotent action-log
replay adapter driving the app's own auth and mutation paths.

**Explicitly not built** (out of scope for a reduced run): M4 (media messages,
reactions, edit/delete), M5 (ephemeral, chat customization, full search scopes),
M6 (offline writes, push seam, custom-client API), M7, M8. No scale replay was
run.

## 7. Candid gap list

Things a grader should know are weaker than they look, in the order I would fix
them.

1. **Table visibility is `public-read`, with app-level scoping in the query
   handlers.** Only declared functions are reachable, and `chatMessages` /
   `chatDetails` return nothing to a non-member, so there is no *reachable* leak
   — but I did not use Snapback's `membership` visibility kind, so there is no
   defence in depth at the storage boundary. This is the first thing I would
   change. (M1–M3 have no assertion covering it and O3 is null on a reduced run,
   which is exactly why it was the easy thing to defer.)
2. **No `authScopeField` on any principal-dependent live query.** Codegen
   rejects a computed-record field name (`FUNCTION_UNKNOWN_FIELD`: it validates
   against the *primary table's* fields), so my per-viewer feed, chat, and
   profile queries carry no scope declaration. The `ctx.auth` gate inside each
   handler is real, but the platform's invalidation and retained-result
   bookkeeping does not know these results are per-principal.
3. **Two bounded reads that will not survive the scale envelope.** The viewer's
   own like/repost projection is `take(1024)` per table per query, and the
   Following-scope feed queries once per followed actor (fine at 8 personas,
   wrong at the brief's 500-follow probe user). Both are honest today and both
   are M6/M8 problems I did not have to solve; I have marked the first in source.
4. **Feed paging caps at six pages (120 entries).** Fixed hook slots were the
   robust fix for a live-update bug; a real client should virtualize.
5. **Receipts are implemented but not asserted end-to-end.** The state machine
   (`sent` → `delivered` → `read`, monotonic, aggregate over the recipient set at
   send time, leavers dropping out) is in `sendMessage`/`markChatState`/
   `aggregateReceipt` and renders through the kit's `ReceiptTicks` with the
   semantic state as its accessible label — but the frozen contract pins no
   semantic receipt token, so the choreography skips it as unimplementable and no
   suite-required assertion covers it. It is code with a UI, not a proven claim.
6. **Group receipt aggregation and member-removal live cutoff** are likewise
   implemented (`removeMember` deletes the membership row, which both stops
   delivery and drops the member from the aggregate requirement) but unproven for
   the same reason.
7. **`sm-profile` and `sm-convo-bubble` are lane-owned wrappers around the kit
   components**, which keep their own testIDs (`sm-profile-card`,
   `sm-convo-bubble-body`). This was necessary — the harness reads the first line
   of `sm-profile` as the display name, and it looks for message actions *inside*
   the selected bubble — and it changes no component contract, but a grader
   comparing against the kit's default IDs should know why they moved.
8. **The `seedRefs` ledger is an application table serving a test concern.** It
   is what makes per-segment idempotency true and reset-safe, and the brief asks
   for a "versioned, idempotent seed", but it is app schema carrying replay
   bookkeeping.
9. **No lockfile discipline across the two package roots.** `clique/bun.lock`
   pins the app; the lane root has a second tiny `package.json`/`bun.lock` that
   bun created for Playwright. Reproducible, but two roots.
10. **`sm-feed-diagnostics` ships in the UI.** It is a small caption showing each
    feed page slot's `status/freshness/connection/rowcount`. I added it to debug
    a staleness bug and kept it because the platform exposes no per-query
    delivery observability; it should be behind a dev flag in a real product.
11. **Timing-sensitive checks are genuinely timing-sensitive.** The M2
    repost-following check passes 1–3 of 3 attempts depending on scheduling; the
    typing check passes 3/3 with ~600 ms of headroom against a 2 s ceiling. Both
    are green, neither is comfortable.
12. **Web only, in practice.** Every milestone produced an iOS Hermes bundle
    export as required, but nothing was run on a simulator or device, and
    `custody: 'durable-required'` is proven here only on the Expo-web
    IndexedDB/Web-Locks carrier.

All three milestones are green and signalled. Run complete.

## Result

**M1, M2, M3 — all `green`**, each requiring both a coverage-validated suite run and a passing choreography segment.

| | Suite (suite-required assertions) | Choreography segment |
|---|---|---|
| **M1** accounts & profiles | 7/7, coverage 7/7 | 3/3 required, `green:true`, `nonGreenCause:null` |
| **M2** posts & follow graph | 22/22, coverage 22/22 | 7/7 required (2 optional contract skips), `green:true` |
| **M3** messaging core | 7/7, coverage 7/7 | 2/2 required + optional quoted-reply (4 contract skips), `green:true` |

Wall by controller window: M1 3,185 s · M2 4,642 s · M3 3,266 s. First-green epochs 1787566147 / 1787570765 / 1787573734.

## What was built

Clique as an Expo Router web app on Snapback 0.1.25 in the default explicit profile — `schema.mjs` (12 tables, a `defineAuth` password program) and `functions.mjs` (~1,300 lines of live queries, mutations, and asset intents), the frozen UI kit vendored verbatim, a fixture action-log replay adapter driving the app's own signup/mutation paths with a `seedRefs` idempotency ledger, and one acceptance entrypoint (`npm run acceptance -- --milestone mN`) that seeds, asserts, validates coverage against the instrument's manifest, and emits the suite-status linkage plus typed observations.

Because M1 and M2 had already been signalled when later changes landed, I re-ran all three suites and all three choreography segments on the final build into separate `regression-*` receipts: M1 7/7, M2 22/22, M3 7/7, all segments green. `tsc --noEmit` clean.

## Attribution, honestly

14 correction loops: **12 agent-error, 1 ambiguous, 0 snapback-defect**, plus 2 environment workarounds (random ports in the supervised Expo loop; read-only instrument tree preventing the harness from installing Playwright — the harness still ran verbatim under a resolve hook). The one ambiguous case is `SNAPBACK_OUTBOX_AUTHORIZATION_SUSPENDED`, whose message says it *waits* for authorization proof while it actually refuses and the caller must wait; the refusal is effect-free, so a bounded retry is safe.

I also recorded a measurement rather than relabelling it: the M2 `repost-following-feed-surface` check samples the other client's feed immediately after the composing client settles, which is a ~50/50 race against ~270 ms live propagation (3/6 in a probe). Best-of-three absorbs it; the failed attempts stay in the receipt.

`diary.md` (three boundary entries), `essay.md` (~1,800 words vs Convex/Supabase/Firebase/hand-rolled), and `final-report.md` (clocks, pins, source-inspection log, 12-item candid gap list, `end=1787574126`) are complete. Servers 82420, 84355, 93615, 86050 were stopped by PID only.
